newsitem.title: FINLAND: FOCUS-Strong upturn for Finland's Merita.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Strong upturn for Finland's Merita.

text.p: Finland's biggest banking group Merita Oy on Wednesday reported sharply higher 1996 earnings and resumed a dividend for the first time since the early 1990s.
Merita said it saw another clear improvement in operating earnings this year.

Reporting operating profit after credit losses up at 1.2 billion markka ($243.3 million) against 491 million in 1995, Merita proposed a 0.20 markka dividend per A share and a 1.60 markka payout per preferred B share.
Both payouts were the first since the early 1990s from either of the banks -- Kansallis-Osake-Pankki KOPF.HE and Unitas Oy -- which merged to form Merita in 1995.
Finland's banks in the early 1990s were plunged into deep crisis as the economy shrank dramatically after they had embarked on a lending bonanza in the late 1980s.

Merita's result was largely in line with expectations -- the median of analysts' forecasts had been for a 1.27 billion markka operating profit in a 1.1 billion to 2.5 billion range -- but Merita's stock still managed to graze new highs in fair trade.

The share, which has risen sharply in recent weeks amid mounting talk that the prospect of a European single currency will force financial institutions to merge, touched 18.40 markka in a few deals, later easing to 17.70, unchanged.
But Merita CEO Vesa Vainio, commenting on the report at a news conference, did nothing to fuel speculation Merita was about to team up with a Nordic or other partner.
Although he said he saw more bank mergers in Europe, he said Merita had not held talks to merge or tighten cooperation with Swedish SE-Banken or any other foreign bank.
"In my view Merita is quite a suitable size for Finland and in a European context also a significant regional player," he said.
Merita said last week it had held unsuccessful merger talks with Finland's top insurers, Sampo and Pohjola.
Merita's net loan and guarantee losses fell to 1.5 billion markka from 1.7 billion in 1995, with net income from financial operations up at 4.1 billion from 3.8 billion.
Vainio said its credit losses were now about normal by international comparison.
The bank said continued low interest rates and a steady improvement in its loan portfolio boded well for 1997.
"The Merita Group expects its operating result to improve clearly in the current year," Vainio said in a statement.
Merita said interest rates were likely to stay low which would reduce its funding costs, and its non-performing receivables and underperforming assets were on a steady, if slower, downward trend.
"Other favourable developments include the decline in one-off integration expenses and the permanent cost benefits derived from the merger, the full impact of which is gradually being felt," it said.
